source: original; stimulus paraphrased from the 1965 education and housing laws

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the 1965 education and housing laws, from the grounding books. The Department of Housing and Urban Development was created by a separate law, the Department of Housing and Urban Development Act, P.L. 89-174, September 9, 1965.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the Great Society's education and housing laws of 1965. The Elementary and Secondary Education Act sent federal grants to schools in poor areas of the country. The Higher Education Act gave federal aid to college students from low-income families. Head Start, begun in 1965, prepared disadvantaged preschool children for school. The Housing and Urban Development Act of 1965 funded housing and urban improvements, and a separate law that year created the Department of Housing and Urban Development to supervise them.

stem: According to the passage, Head Start was designed to

options.text: prepare disadvantaged preschool children for school
train high school graduates for factory jobs
options.misconception: Head Start prepared preschool children for school; it did not train graduates for factory jobs.

options.text: build new housing for low-income families
options.misconception: Building housing was the work of the housing law, not of Head Start.

options.text: give college aid to students from wealthy families
options.misconception: The Higher Education Act aided students from low-income families, and Head Start served preschool children.

rationales.A: The passage says Head Start prepared disadvantaged preschool children for school.
rationales.B: Head Start prepared preschool children for school; it did not train graduates for factory jobs.
rationales.C: Building housing was the work of the housing law, not of Head Start.
rationales.D: The Higher Education Act aided students from low-income families, and Head Start served preschool children.
rationales.general:
1. Head Start served preschool children, the youngest students.
2. Those children came from disadvantaged homes.
3. The program prepared them for school before they started.
4. Head Start therefore gave poor children a head start on learning.
5. A child who starts school ready to learn has a better chance, and poor children start with less.
Remember: A program's age group tells you its purpose.
